title: Compressed and differential timestamps
summary: Understand why vector metadata can be compressed and compare naive quadratic storage with a differential linear-order technique.
objectives: Explain the storage overhead of recent timestamp tables

sections.title: Send only what changed
sections.body: A sender can piggyback only vector entries that differ from the last timestamp sent to that receiver. The receiver applies maxima to the transmitted components before updating and delivering the message.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: Compression is examinable as an implementation bridge: preserve causal information while reducing repeated metadata.

sections.title: Differential storage trade-off
sections.body: The receiver-specific recent-timestamp table can require quadratic storage. The Singhal-Kshemkalyani technique keeps last-sent and last-updated vectors to reduce storage to linear order while still identifying changed entries.

sourceLens.whyExaminable: This topic tests systems reasoning: a correctness-preserving optimization changes metadata state and storage complexity.

examples.title: Metadata delta trace
steps: Store the last vector sent to the target process.
Update the current vector before sending.
Update the receiver with componentwise maxima and then deliver.
examples.answer: Compression changes representation and storage, not the causal meaning of the delivered message.

contrastDrills.prompt: What does a compressed timestamp omit?
choices: Entries unchanged since the last message to that receiver
contrastDrills.explanation: The compressed representation omits repeated entries that the receiver already knows from a prior message.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which technique is introduced as reducing timestamp storage from quadratic order to linear order?
contrastDrills.explanation: The differential technique maintains last-sent and last-updated vectors instead of a receiver-specific table of recent vectors.
contrastDrills.misconception: Name the ordering, time, or communication boundary before choosing.

math.explanation: Keeping a recent vector timestamp for every sender-receiver pair creates quadratic storage in the number of processes.
math.name: Recent-vector storage cost
math.purpose: Use it as the quadratic metadata baseline before introducing differential compression.

math.explanation: The Singhal-Kshemkalyani differential technique reduces storage by maintaining only Last Sent and Last Update vectors at each process.
math.name: Differential timestamp storage cost
math.purpose: Use it to explain how receiver-specific Last Sent and Last Update state targets linear storage.

criticalQuestions.prompt: What must remain invariant when timestamp metadata is compressed?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate representation size from the causal information needed by the receiver.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The receiver must still be able to reconstruct the relevant componentwise causal knowledge; compression may omit repetition but not required dependencies.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is receiver-specific state needed in the basic compressed scheme?
criticalQuestions.angle: The sender must know what this particular receiver has already observed.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Different receivers may have received different prior vectors, so the set of changed entries depends on the destination.
